title: Genetics Fundamentals
summary: This lesson introduces the structure and function of DNA and genes, and explains how traits are passed from parents to offspring. Students will learn basic inheritance patterns and practice using simple Punnett squares.

sections.heading: What Is DNA?
sections.body:
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a long molecule that stores the genetic instructions for building and maintaining an organism. It looks like a twisted ladder, called a double helix, where the sides are sugar‑phosphate backbones and the rungs are pairs of bases (A with T, C with G). These base pairs form the code that determines an organism's traits.

Each segment of DNA that contains the instructions for a single trait is called a gene. Genes are like recipes: they tell cells how to make proteins, which perform most of the work in the body.

sections.heading: How Traits Are Inherited
sections.body:
Every individual receives two copies of each gene—one from the mother and one from the father. The version of a gene is called an allele. If the alleles are the same, the individual is homozygous; if they differ, the individual is heterozygous.

Traits can be dominant or recessive. A dominant allele masks the effect of a recessive allele in a heterozygous pair, so the dominant trait appears in the offspring.

Mendel’s law of segregation states that the two alleles for a gene separate during the formation of gametes (sperm or egg), so each gamete carries only one allele for each gene.

sections.heading: Simple Punnett Squares
sections.body:
A Punnett square is a grid that helps predict the possible genotypes and phenotypes of offspring. To draw one, write the parental alleles on the top and side of a 2×2 box, then fill in each square by combining the alleles.

Example: If both parents are heterozygous for flower colour (Rr, where R = red dominant, r = white recessive), the Punnett square shows ¼ RR, ½ Rr, and ¼ rr. This predicts a 75% chance of red flowers and a 25% chance of white flowers in the offspring.

Punnett squares work for single‑gene traits; more complex traits need larger grids or different methods.

key_terms.meaning: The molecule that carries genetic information in all living cells.
A segment of DNA that codes for a specific protein or trait.
One of two or more versions of a gene.
An allele that expresses its trait even when paired with a different allele.
An allele that only shows its trait when paired with an identical allele.

quiz.q: What are the two nitrogen bases that pair together in DNA?
quiz.why: A always pairs with T in DNA.

quiz.q: If a trait is recessive, which genotype will show the trait?
quiz.why: Only the homozygous recessive genotype expresses a recessive trait.

quiz.q: In a cross between two heterozygous parents (Rr × Rr), what fraction of the offspring are expected to be heterozygous?
quiz.why: A 2×2 Punnett square gives 2 out of 4 squares as Rr, which is 1/2.

quiz.q: Mendel’s law of segregation explains that:
quiz.why: The law states that each gamete receives only one allele of each gene.
